desc:
A factory has n robots in a row. Robot i needs charge[i] units of charge to start and then costs running[i] units per hour to run. You choose a group of consecutive robots and run them together. Starting them all costs only the largest charge in the group, and running them costs the sum of their running costs times the group size:

cost(group) = max(charge in group) + size * sum(running in group)

Return the largest group size whose cost is at most budget, or 0 if even a single robot is too expensive.

charge = [4, 2, 7, 3], running = [1, 2, 1, 2], budget = 19
[4,2,7]: 7 + 3 * (1+2+1) = 19  -> allowed
no group of 4 fits (7 + 4 * 6 = 31)
result = 3
hints: Compute the cost of any single group directly, then ask how the cost changes when a group grows. Checking all O(n<sup>2</sup>) groups is the baseline.
Adding a robot to a group never lowers its cost (the maximum, the sum and the size can only go up). So if a group is affordable, every smaller group inside it is too, and a sliding window works.

While extending the window to the right, maintain the sum of running costs and a decreasing deque of charges for the maximum. If the cost exceeds the budget, move the left end forward (removing the front of the deque when it leaves) until the window is affordable again.
editorial: The cost function is monotone: for groups A ⊂ B, cost(A) ≤ cost(B), since all three ingredients (maximum charge, number of robots, total running cost) are non-decreasing when robots are added. Therefore for each right end r the set of affordable left ends is a suffix l..r, and the smallest affordable l never moves left as r grows. That is exactly the two-pointer window pattern.

Maintain the running sum of the window and a monotonic deque of charge indices (decreasing values) to get the window maximum in O(1). After adding robot r, while charge[deque front] + (r - l + 1) * sum > budget, remove robot l: subtract its running cost and pop the deque front if it is l. The window can become empty when a single robot is too expensive. Track the largest window size seen. O(n) time, O(n) space.
